lesson.title: Reading the T-Table: Finding Your Critical Value
lesson.summary: A t critical value depends on both the confidence level (or alpha) and the degrees of freedom, and for any given confidence level it is always at least as large as the corresponding z critical value.
lesson.body:
A critical value marks the boundary of the region considered unusual enough to reject a null hypothesis, or, for a confidence interval, the number of standard errors needed to reach a target confidence level. For a t-distribution, finding this boundary, written t*, requires two pieces of information rather than one: the confidence level, or significance level alpha, you want, and the degrees of freedom, since the exact shape of the t-distribution changes with df. This is different from a z critical value, which depends only on the confidence level, because there is only one standard normal curve.

Suppose you have a sample of size n = 12, so degrees of freedom is n - 1 = 11, and you want a 95 percent confidence level, which corresponds to a two-sided alpha of 0.05 split evenly, 0.025 in each tail. Looking this up in a t-table at df = 11 and a two-tail probability of 0.05 gives t* = 2.201. Compare this to the z critical value for the same 95 percent confidence level, z* = 1.960. The t critical value is noticeably larger. This is a direct, numerical consequence of the heavier tails discussed in the previous section: because more probability sits in the tails of a t-distribution, you have to go farther out from the center to enclose the same amount of area, 95 percent in this case, so t* is always at least as large as z* for a matching confidence level.

This gap between t* and z* shrinks as degrees of freedom increases, exactly mirroring the way the t-distribution itself approaches the normal curve. At df = 30, the 95 percent t critical value is 2.042, closer to 1.960 than the df = 11 value was. At very large df, t* essentially equals 1.960. Because of this, most t-tables include a bottom row labeled with infinity as the degrees of freedom, which lists exactly the z critical values, a reminder that the t-distribution becomes the standard normal distribution in that limit. When you look up a critical value, always match both the correct df and the correct tail probability for your confidence level or alpha, since using the wrong one of either silently changes your answer.
